title: The Campus Drug Problem Is Still Alcohol
hook: A cocaine bust makes the news; the drug actually harming college students doesn't. Cocaine use among young adults is down — heavy drinking is what the research keeps pointing at.
key_points: Cocaine use among young adults has declined in recent survey data.
Heavy alcohol use remains the dominant substance risk on college campuses.
Dramatic enforcement stories skew perception toward the rarer drug.
Alcohol's harms are spread across many people rather than concentrated in a few headlines.
Binge drinking drives injuries, assaults, and academic and health consequences.
Prevention effort tends to follow attention rather than actual harm.
content_html: A drug bust at a university makes for a clean story: a ring, an arrest, a number. It's also a poor guide to what's actually hurting students. Survey data show cocaine use among young adults declining, while heavy drinking remains the substance problem that consistently shows up in campus injury, assault, and health statistics.
extra_html:
The gap is a familiar failure of risk perception. Alcohol's harm arrives distributed — one fall, one alcohol-poisoning ER visit, one assault, one semester derailed, spread across thousands of separate nights and never adding up to a single event anyone reports. An illicit-drug ring is one event with a name attached. Attention follows the second, and prevention budgets tend to follow attention.

None of this makes cocaine safe, and the decline is worth noting rather than assuming. The point is where the leverage sits: for the average student, the meaningful question isn't whether there's a dealer on campus, it's how many drinks are in a typical night out.

related.title: Alcohol and Your Health
related.hook: There's no amount of alcohol proven to be good for you — but there's a meaningful difference between a glass with dinner and patterns that quietly raise your risk of cancer, liver disease, and more.

related.title: Understanding Addiction
related.hook: Addiction isn't a lack of willpower or a moral failing — it's a treatable medical condition that changes how the brain works. And like other chronic illnesses, it responds to treatment.

related.title: Drinking to Cope With Stress May Permanently Rewire the Brain
related.hook: Using alcohol to cope with stress at a young age may permanently change the brain — making it harder to adapt to future challenges and raising the risk of drinking again later in life.

related.title: Wine, Beer, or Spirits — Does the Drink Matter?
related.hook: In 340,000 adults tracked for a decade, heavy drinking raised mortality no matter what was in the glass. At lower intakes, wine looked different from beer and spirits.

flashcards.prompt: What substance poses the largest risk to college students, per the research?
flashcards.back_html: Alcohol — particularly heavy and binge drinking. Cocaine use among young adults has actually been declining.

flashcards.prompt: Why does alcohol get less attention than a campus cocaine bust?

choices.text: Its harm is spread thinly across many students rather than concentrated in one dramatic event
Alcohol causes fewer total injuries than cocaine on campuses
Alcohol use among students has fallen to near zero

flashcards.explanation_html: A bust is a single vivid story; alcohol harm arrives as many separate injuries, assaults, and health consequences that never aggregate into one headline.
